summary: This document specifies the Host Access Protocol, designed as the network-access protocol for the Wideband Packet Satellite Network and intended to evolve toward other networks such as SATNET. The RFC itself calls HAP an experimental protocol that would be revised.

eli5.summary: This is the way a computer talks to a satellite network to send its data up and down. It was still being tested and changed.

subtitle: How a host talks to a packet-switched satellite network over its access link: datagrams, streams, groups and link control.

tldr.problem: A host connected to a packet-switched satellite network needs an agreed way to send data and control messages to its dedicated packet-switching computer, which must also offer satellite-specific options such as guaranteed bandwidth, priorities and group delivery.
tldr.mechanism: HAP defines 16-bit-word message formats for datagrams, streams and control messages exchanged over the host-to-SIMP access link, plus an acceptance/refusal flow control scheme, setup exchanges for streams and groups, and procedures for link restart, monitoring and loopback.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls HAP experimental and expects it to be revised. It was written for the Wideband Packet Satellite Network and meant to evolve toward SATNET and similar networks. The index lists it as an Internet Standard updated by RFC 1221.

today: The index lists RFC 907 as an Internet Standard that has been updated by RFC 1221, although the text itself calls HAP an experimental protocol that would be revised. It describes the access protocol designed for the Wideband Packet Satellite Network.

sections.title: What the Host Access Protocol Does
sections.content:
The Host Access Protocol (HAP) defines network-access level communication between a computer, called a host, and a packet-switched satellite network. The host connects over an access link to a dedicated packet-switching computer called a Satellite Interface Message Processor (Satellite IMP, or SIMP). HAP sets out the control messages and host-to-host data messages that can cross that link, their formats, and when each should be sent.

SIMPs differ from ARPANET IMPs: they form a network through connections to a common multiaccess and broadcast satellite channel, rather than dedicated point-to-point terrestrial lines. That changes how messages are delivered and which service options the network can offer.

The Preface says HAP was originally designed as the network-access level protocol for the DARPA/DCA sponsored Wideband Packet Satellite Network. It was intended to evolve into a standard interface for satellite networks such as SATNET and TACNET (aka MATNET). It is a minor revision of, and supersedes, Chapter 4 of BBN Report No. 4469, the PSAT Technical Report. The new items are the Loopback Request, Link Going Down and NOP control messages, a Reason field in Restart Request, new Unnumbered Response codes, and new setup code values. The earlier SATNET and MATNET interface was the Host/SATNET Protocol, documented in IEN 192.

The protocol that makes the host-SIMP link reliable enough is assumed to sit below HAP. The RFC gives ARPANET 1822, the ARPANET VDH protocol and HDLC as examples.
sections.eli5: A big computer plugs into a special mail-sorting computer that sends messages through a satellite. HAP is the language those two use to talk to each other.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.content:
HAP is a full duplex, non-reliable protocol with an optional flow control mechanism. It does not guarantee error-free sequenced delivery; if the link needs that, the link-level protocol underneath must supply it. Every HAP message is a whole number of 16-bit words. Word 0 identifies the message type and word 1 is a checksum over the header, and a message whose header checksum does not match must be discarded.

There are two kinds of data message. Datagram messages are the basic service, with a nominal two satellite hop delay of about 0.6 sec between hosts on different SIMPs. Stream messages give a one satellite hop delay (about 0.3 sec) for volatile traffic such as speech, or guaranteed channel bandwidth for high duty cycle applications. Each can be up to approximately 16K bits long. Hosts have permanent 16-bit logical addresses that are independent of the SIMP port they use, and they can join groups for multi-destination delivery such as conferencing.

Other features include three reliability levels (low, medium, high) that choose the forward error correction used on the satellite channel, an optional per-message choice to discard or deliver messages with data errors, four priority classes from 3 (highest) to 0 (lowest), and an acceptance/refusal mechanism for flow control. HAP can also be seen as a message layer, for individual datagrams and streams, and a setup layer, for creating, changing and deleting streams and groups.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of delivery: a normal letter that takes a bit longer, and a reserved fast lane for things like voice. You can also send to a whole club at once.

sections.title: Datagram and Stream Message Headers
sections.content:
A datagram message has a six-word header followed by up to 16,384 bits (1024 16-bit words) of user data. Word 0 holds the message class bit (0 for data, 1 for control), a loopback bit (0 sent by host, 1 sent by SIMP), a 2-bit Go-Priority field that advises the lowest priority the SIMP is currently accepting, a force-channel-transmission flag, and an 8-bit message number used by acceptance/refusal. A message number of zero turns acceptance/refusal off for that message. Word 1 is the header checksum, the negation of the 2's-complement sum of words 0 to 5 excluding the checksum word. Word 2 can carry a piggybacked acceptance/refusal word.

Word 3 carries the data message type bit (0 datagram, 1 stream), an Internet/Local flag saying whether the data begins with a standard DoD Internet header, a Discard flag and Data Error flag for handling data errors, a 2-bit Time-to-Live (1, 2, 5 or 10 seconds), a 2-bit priority, a 2-bit reliability and a 6-bit reliability length. The reliability length lets the first words of user data, such as private IP and TCP headers, be sent at the highest reliability. Words 4 and 5 are the destination and source host addresses.

A stream message has the same six-word shape, but word 3 holds a 10-bit Host Stream ID in place of priority, reliability and reliability length, because those are fixed when the stream is created. Its time-to-live can only be 1 second, and it carries up to 16,000 bits of data. The destination address can differ from message to message, so one stream can multiplex several logical flows. Stream messages must match the stream allocation in both size and interarrival time to be efficient.
sections.eli5: Each letter has an envelope with boxes to fill in: who it is for, who it is from, how important it is, how careful the carrier must be, and a number so the clerk can say yes or no to it.

sections.title: Acceptance and Refusal Flow Control
sections.content:
The acceptance/refusal (A/R) mechanism lets the receiver of a message tell the sender what happened to it locally. It works in each direction on the access link and is enabled by a bit in the Restart Complete message. Messages are numbered modulo 256 and up to 127 may be outstanding in each direction. A refusal carries the message number and a reason, and may be piggybacked on a data message going the other way or sent in a separate control message.

An acceptance only means the message was not refused. It does not guarantee delivery, and the network may still discard the message later; it exists mainly to help the host manage buffers. A single A/R can cover earlier outstanding messages, so accepting message N implicitly accepts N-1, N-2 and so on, and a block of A/R words can be packed into one control message.

When the overhead is not worth it, A/R can be disabled so the interface works in a pure discard mode. Critical feedback can still be sent in an Unnumbered Response control message, which reports problems such as an unreachable destination, an illegal host address, a nonexistent stream ID or a protocol violation. A/R controls individual messages, while the Go-Priority field in headers gives advisory information about which priorities are currently being accepted, so senders can avoid messages that are sure to be refused.
sections.eli5: The clerk can say 'got it' or 'sorry, I cannot take that, and here is why' for each letter, or for a batch of letters at once. You can also turn this off if you do not want the chatter.

sections.title: Setting Up Streams and Groups
sections.content:
Streams and groups are created, changed and deleted by talking to the network service host, which has logical address zero. These setup messages are special datagrams. A host-initiated exchange has three steps: the host sends a Request with a unique Request ID, the service host returns a Reply, and the host returns a Reply Acknowledgment. SIMP-initiated Notifications, such as a stream being suspended, resumed or deleted, take two steps: the Notification and a Notification Acknowledgment. A reply to a global request should arrive within 2 seconds and to a local one within 1 second, and the host should acknowledge a Reply within 1 second.

Each stream has six properties chosen at setup: slot size, interval, reliability, reliability length, priority, and maximum messages per slot. The interval is counted in 21.2 ms frames, and the RFC gives 4 frames as an allocation of Slot Size words every 85 ms. After a successful Create Stream Reply with reply code 0, the host may send stream messages using the Host Stream ID the network assigned. All properties except the interval can be changed later. A host asking for less capacity should slow down at once, but one asking for more must wait for reply code 4.

A group address supports multi-destination delivery. The creating host receives a 16-bit group address and a 48-bit key, and must pass both to the other hosts it wants as members, outside HAP. The key authenticates Join, Leave and Delete operations. Leave is local and just removes the host from the member list. Delete removes the group from every SIMP, and any member may delete a group at any time. Data sent to a group always travels over the satellite channel.
sections.eli5: To get a reserved fast lane or a group chat, you fill in a request form for the main office. They reply and you confirm. For a group, you get a secret key that you must share with friends so they can join.

sections.title: Link Initialization, Monitoring and Loopback
sections.content:
Link initialization uses a Restart Request (RR) and Restart Complete (RC) exchange. Both host and SIMP must implement the five-state diagram (OFF, INIT, RR-SNT, RC-SNT, ON) to avoid deadlocks and oscillations. All states have 10-second timeouts that return to OFF. An RR resets monitoring statistics and stops all traffic in both directions; an RC reply shows the link works both ways and carries the bit that enables or disables A/R. A restart reason field gives power up, system restart, link restart, link timeout or loopback timeout.

While the link runs, host and SIMP must exchange Status messages once a second. These carry the most recent A/R word, stream capacity (SIMP only), a timestamp and counters of messages sent, received without errors, received with errors, bad header checksums and hardware error indications, so each end can compute link performance. The status messages also support the Network Operations Center (NOC).

A Loopback Request asks the other end to return all of the sender's messages unmodified for a set number of seconds, either at the interface hardware or at the driver software. The requester waits for a 10-second timer, a Can't implement loop response, or one of its own reflected messages. Other control messages are Link Going Down, which warns of a planned shutdown with a reason and times in minutes, and NOP, which carries up to 32 words of undefined data and may be needed to clear link hardware state.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two sides shake hands to make sure the wire works in both directions. Then they check in every second, and a repair crew can ask for a mirror test where everything sent comes straight back.

sections.title: Status of the Specification
sections.content:
The Preface describes HAP as an experimental protocol that will be revised as new capabilities are added and different satellite networks are supported. It says implementations should be done in coordination with satellite network development and operations personnel, and that the details of this version most closely match the Wideband Satellite Network.

The RFC contains no security section. The only protection it describes is the 48-bit group key that authenticates group operations, so that unwanted hosts do not deliberately or inadvertently become members.
sections.eli5: The authors said this was a work in progress that they would keep changing as new satellites and new needs came along.
